overview.text: An alloy is a material made by combining two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal; it is not limited to mixtures of two metals, since steel includes carbon, a nonmetal. In many alloys, atoms either replace some atoms in a metal’s crystal arrangement (a substitutional alloy) or smaller atoms fit into spaces between them (an interstitial alloy). These arrangements, along with the proportions of ingredients, can give an alloy properties different from those of its ingredients. Alloying helps tailor materials for particular uses: bronze (copper and tin), brass (copper and zinc), and steel (iron with carbon and often other elements) are familiar examples used in tools, instruments, and structures.

key_facts.text: An alloy contains at least two elements, including at least one metal; the other element can be a nonmetal, as carbon is in steel.
In substitutional alloys, some atoms take the place of metal atoms in the crystal structure; in interstitial alloys, smaller atoms fit between them.
Bronze is made from copper and tin; compared with copper, it is harder and easier to cast.
Brass is made from copper and zinc and is used in musical instruments; its malleability and acoustic properties are useful for this purpose.
Steel is primarily iron with carbon and may include elements such as chromium, manganese, or nickel; different steel alloys are used for strength, hardness, or corrosion resistance.
